intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal recessive severe congenital neutropenia-14 (SCN14) is caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutation in the CSF3 gene, which encodes colony-stimulating factor 3 (granulocyte colony-stimulating factor, G-CSF).

checks.claim: Autosomal recessive severe congenital neutropenia-14 (SCN14) is caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutation in the CSF3 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Our results suggest that CSF3 deficiency in humans causes a novel autosomal recessive form of SCN.
checks.explanation: The abstract describes biallelic inactivating CSF3 variants that cause a novel autosomal recessive form of SCN. The SCN14 label is OMIM's own name for this disease.

checks.claim: The CSF3 gene encodes colony-stimulating factor 3, also known as granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF).
checks.evidence_quote: Colony-stimulating factor 3 (CSF3) is a key factor in neutrophil production and function
checks.explanation: The abstract names the gene product as colony-stimulating factor 3. It does not mention the alias granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF).

paragraphs.text: Autosomal recessive severe congenital neutropenia-14 (SCN14) is a form of severe congenital neutropenia caused by complete deficiency of colony-stimulating factor 3 (CSF3), a key factor in neutrophil production and function. Khouj et al. (2023) noted that the phenotype mirrors that documented in mouse and zebrafish models of CSF3 deficiency.

checks.claim: SCN14 is a form of severe congenital neutropenia caused by complete deficiency of colony-stimulating factor 3 (CSF3).
checks.evidence_quote: Complete deficiency of CSF3 as a result of nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) could be demonstrated on RT-PCR using skin fibroblasts-derived RNA.
checks.explanation: The abstract reports complete CSF3 deficiency and says CSF3 deficiency causes a novel form of SCN.

checks.claim: CSF3 is a key factor in neutrophil production and function.
checks.evidence_quote: Colony-stimulating factor 3 (CSF3) is a key factor in neutrophil production and function

checks.claim: Khouj et al. (2023) noted that the SCN14 phenotype mirrors the phenotype documented in mouse and zebrafish models of CSF3 deficiency.
checks.evidence_quote: The phenotype observed in this cohort mirrors that documented in mouse and zebrafish models of CSF3 deficiency.

paragraphs.text: The transmission pattern of SCN14 in the families reported by Khouj et al. (2023) was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance. Almannai et al. (2026) reported a further patient with a homozygous loss-of-function variant in CSF3, supporting autosomal recessive inheritance.

checks.claim: The transmission pattern of SCN14 in the families reported by Khouj et al. (2023) was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.
checks.evidence_quote: three patients from two families each segregating a different biallelic inactivating variant in CSF3 with SCN
checks.explanation: Both families segregate biallelic variants, and the authors conclude the disease is autosomal recessive.

checks.claim: Almannai et al. (2026) reported an additional SCN14 patient with a homozygous loss-of-function variant in CSF3.
checks.evidence_quote: We present the first confirmatory report of a previously proposed SCN due to a homozygous pathogenic loss-of-function variant in CSF3.
checks.explanation: The abstract confirms an additional report of SCN with a homozygous loss-of-function variant in CSF3. It does not state the number of patients and does not use the SCN14 label.

checks.claim: The homozygous CSF3 loss-of-function variant in the patient reported by Almannai et al. (2026) supports autosomal recessive inheritance of SCN14.
checks.evidence_quote: Further Support of Autosomal Recessive CSF3-Related Severe Congenital Neutropenia.
checks.explanation: The title and abstract present the homozygous variant as support for autosomal recessive CSF3-related SCN.

paragraphs.text: In 3 patients from 2 families with severe congenital neutropenia, Khouj et al. (2023) identified biallelic inactivating variants in the CSF3 gene; each family segregated a different variant. RT-PCR analysis of RNA derived from patient skin fibroblasts demonstrated complete deficiency of CSF3 as a result of nonsense-mediated decay. Khouj et al. (2023) noted that biallelic inactivation of the CSF3 receptor, CSF3R, was already a well-established cause of SCN, but that no Mendelian disease had previously been ascribed to CSF3.

checks.claim: Khouj et al. (2023) studied 3 patients from 2 families with severe congenital neutropenia.
checks.evidence_quote: Here, we describe three patients from two families each segregating a different biallelic inactivating variant in CSF3 with SCN.
checks.explanation: The abstract states 3 patients from 2 families.

checks.claim: Khouj et al. (2023) identified biallelic inactivating variants in the CSF3 gene in 3 patients from 2 families with severe congenital neutropenia.
checks.evidence_quote: Here, we describe three patients from two families each segregating a different biallelic inactivating variant in CSF3 with SCN.

checks.claim: Each of the 2 families with severe congenital neutropenia reported by Khouj et al. (2023) segregated a different CSF3 variant.
checks.evidence_quote: two families each segregating a different biallelic inactivating variant in CSF3

checks.claim: RT-PCR analysis of RNA from skin fibroblasts of patients with biallelic CSF3 variants demonstrated complete deficiency of CSF3.
checks.evidence_quote: Complete deficiency of CSF3 as a result of nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) could be demonstrated on RT-PCR using skin fibroblasts-derived RNA.

checks.claim: The complete CSF3 deficiency in patient fibroblasts with biallelic CSF3 variants resulted from nonsense-mediated decay.
checks.evidence_quote: Complete deficiency of CSF3 as a result of nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) could be demonstrated on RT-PCR using skin fibroblasts-derived RNA.

checks.claim: Khouj et al. (2023) noted that biallelic inactivation of the CSF3 receptor gene, CSF3R, was already a well-established cause of severe congenital neutropenia.
checks.evidence_quote: Although biallelic inactivation of its receptor CSF3R is a well-established cause of severe congenital neutropenia (SCN)

checks.evidence_quote: no corresponding Mendelian disease has been ascribed to date to CSF3.

paragraphs.text: Almannai et al. (2026) reported a patient with severe congenital neutropenia who carried a homozygous pathogenic loss-of-function variant in the CSF3 gene, providing the first confirmatory report of CSF3-related autosomal recessive SCN.

checks.claim: Almannai et al. (2026) reported a patient with severe congenital neutropenia who carried a homozygous pathogenic loss-of-function variant in the CSF3 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: We present the first confirmatory report of a previously proposed SCN due to a homozygous pathogenic loss-of-function variant in CSF3.
checks.explanation: The abstract supports SCN due to a homozygous pathogenic loss-of-function variant in CSF3. It does not say explicitly that a single patient was reported; this may be in the full text.

checks.claim: The report by Almannai et al. (2026) was the first confirmatory report of CSF3-related autosomal recessive severe congenital neutropenia.
checks.evidence_quote: We present the first confirmatory report of a previously proposed SCN due to a homozygous pathogenic loss-of-function variant in CSF3.
checks.explanation: The abstract states that this is the first confirmatory report, and the title identifies the disorder as autosomal recessive.

paragraphs.text: Lieschke et al. (1994) generated mice lacking G-CSF by targeted disruption of the G-CSF gene. G-CSF-null mice were viable, fertile, and superficially healthy but had chronic neutropenia, with peripheral blood neutrophil levels 20% to 30% of those of wildtype mice; heterozygous mice had intermediate neutrophil levels, suggesting a gene-dosage effect. In the marrow of null mice, granulopoietic precursor cells were reduced by 50%, and granulocyte, macrophage, and blast progenitor cells were reduced, although mature neutrophils were still present in blood and marrow. Null mice had reduced numbers of neutrophils available for rapid mobilization by a single dose of G-CSF. G-CSF administration reversed the granulopoietic defect: 1 day of treatment raised circulating neutrophil levels to normal, and after 4 days wildtype and null marrows were morphologically indistinguishable. G-CSF-null mice had a markedly impaired ability to control infection with Listeria monocytogenes, with diminished neutrophil and delayed monocyte increases in the blood and reduced infection-driven granulopoiesis.
